books.title: Ganita Prakash: Textbook of Mathematics for Grade 8 (Part-I)
Ganita Prakash: Textbook of Mathematics for Grade 8 (Part-II)
books.edition: First Edition December 2025 (no "Reprint 2026-27" mark in the PDF; the only Part-II edition in the live catalogue)

source.method: chapter titles from the book's Contents page; topics from each chapter PDF's section headings

topics.title: Square Numbers
objectives: Student can explain why numbers like 1, 4, 9, 16 are called squares using areas of squares
Student can use the locker puzzle to see that square numbers have an odd number of factors
visualIdeas: a row of 100 lockers with only the square-numbered lockers left open

topics.title: Patterns and Properties of Perfect Squares
objectives: Student can state that perfect squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9
Student can explain why a square can have only an even number of zeros at the end
visualIdeas: a table of squares 1 to 30 with the units digits highlighted

topics.title: Perfect Squares and Odd Numbers
objectives: Student can show that adding consecutive odd numbers starting from 1 gives consecutive squares
Student can explain the pattern with inverted L-shapes added to a square
visualIdeas: dots arranged in nested L-shapes growing a square

topics.title: Perfect Squares and Triangular Numbers
objectives: Student can show that the sum of two consecutive triangular numbers is a square
Student can extend the pattern and draw the next term showing two triangular numbers forming a square
visualIdeas: two triangular dot arrangements fitting together into a square

topics.title: Square Roots
objectives: Student can find the square root of a perfect square and state that it has a positive and a negative square root
Student can test whether a number is a perfect square by pairing its prime factors
Student can estimate the square root of a number that is not a perfect square by finding the nearest squares
visualIdeas: a square of area 49 sq cm with side 7 cm
a number line between 15 and 16 locating the square root of 250

topics.title: Cubic Numbers
objectives: Student can explain why 1, 8, 27 ... are called perfect cubes using unit cubes
Student can decide whether a number is a perfect cube
visualIdeas: a 3 by 3 by 3 cube built from 27 unit cubes

topics.title: Taxicab Numbers
objectives: Student can recount the Hardy-Ramanujan story of 1729
Student can verify that 1729 is a sum of two cubes in two different ways
visualIdeas: the taxicab number 1729 shown as 1 cubed plus 12 cubed and 9 cubed plus 10 cubed

topics.title: Perfect Cubes and Consecutive Odd Numbers
objectives: Student can describe how groups of consecutive odd numbers add up to perfect cubes
Student can use the pattern to find a sum without calculating it
visualIdeas: rows of odd numbers, 1; 3+5; 7+9+11, each row labelled with its cube

topics.title: Cube Roots
objectives: Student can find the cube root of a perfect cube
Student can test whether a number is a perfect cube by splitting its prime factors into three identical groups
visualIdeas: 3375 written as three identical groups of 3 times 5

topics.title: Successive Differences
objectives: Student can compute successive differences of squares and of cubes until the differences become equal
Student can describe the pattern seen at each level
visualIdeas: a difference table for 1, 8, 27, 64, 125 reaching a constant row

topics.title: A Pinch of History
objectives: Student can state that Babylonian clay tablets listed squares and cubes around 1700 BCE
Student can explain the Sanskrit terms varga for square and ghana for cube
visualIdeas: a clay tablet of square numbers beside the words varga and ghana

topics.title: An Impossible Venture!
objectives: Student can explain how the thickness of a paper doubles with each fold
Student can estimate how quickly repeated doubling becomes very large
visualIdeas: a sheet of paper folded again and again with its thickness doubling at each step

topics.title: Exponential Notation and Operations
objectives: Student can write repeated multiplication in exponential notation, naming the base and the exponent
Student can evaluate expressions such as 0.001 cm x 2 to the power 7
visualIdeas: the paper-folding thickness written as 0.001 x 2 x 2 x 2 and as 0.001 x 2 cubed

topics.title: The Stones that Shine and the Magical Pond
objectives: Student can model repeated tripling and doubling with powers
Student can use the rules that multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents and that a power of a power multiplies them
visualIdeas: a branching tree of daughters, baskets, keys and rooms each multiplying by 3
a pond of lotuses doubling every day

topics.title: How Many Combinations
objectives: Student can count combinations of choices by multiplying the number of options
Student can express the number of possible passwords as a power
visualIdeas: a tree diagram of 4 dresses and 3 caps giving 12 outfits

topics.title: The Other Side of Powers
objectives: Student can divide powers with the same base by subtracting exponents
Student can explain why any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1
Student can write negative exponents as reciprocals, such as 2 to the power -1 equals one half
visualIdeas: a line of 16 units being halved again and again
a power line of 4 from 4 to the power -2 up to 4 to the power 8

topics.title: Powers of 10
objectives: Student can write a number in expanded form using powers of 10
Student can write decimals using negative powers of 10
visualIdeas: 47561 split into place-value blocks labelled 10 to the power 4 down to 10 to the power 0

topics.title: Scientific Notation
objectives: Student can write very large numbers in scientific notation x times 10 to the power y with x at least 1 and less than 10
Student can compare large quantities written in scientific notation
visualIdeas: the distance from the Sun to the galaxy centre written in full and as 3 x 10 to the power 20 m

topics.title: Did You Ever Wonder?
objectives: Student can solve estimation problems by describing relationships among quantities and making reasonable assumptions
Student can carry out approximate calculations for real situations such as donations equal to a person's weight
visualIdeas: a balance scale with a person on one side and sacks of jaggery on the other

topics.title: Linear Growth vs. Exponential Growth
objectives: Student can contrast additive (linear) growth with multiplicative (exponential) growth
Student can compare the steps of a ladder to the Moon with the number of paper folds needed to reach it
visualIdeas: two graphs, one rising in a straight line and one curving steeply upward

topics.title: Getting a Sense for Large Numbers
objectives: Student can relate lakh, crore and arab to million and billion using powers of 10
Student can use powers of 10 to compare very large quantities from the real world
visualIdeas: a number line in powers of 10 marking a lakh, a crore, a billion and beyond

topics.title: A Pinch of History
objectives: Student can describe how ancient Indian texts such as the Lalitavistara named very large powers of ten
Student can compare the Indian naming of large numbers (lakh, crore, arab, kharab) with the international system (million, billion, trillion)
visualIdeas: a scroll listing names for powers of ten up to 10 to the power 53

topics.title: Reema's Curiosity
objectives: Student can describe how a Mesopotamian tablet led Reema to wonder how people wrote numbers in the past
Student can explain why we need a standard way to represent numbers
visualIdeas: an old paper with wedge-shaped symbols slipping out of a book

topics.title: The Mechanism of Counting
objectives: Student can compare collections without number names using one-to-one matching, for example with sticks
Student can explain what a number system is: a standard sequence of objects, names or symbols in a fixed order
visualIdeas: a herd of cows matched one-to-one with a pile of sticks

topics.title: Some Early Number Systems: Body Parts, Tally Marks and Counting in Twos
objectives: Student can describe counting with body parts and with tally marks on bones
Student can explain how the Gumulgal number names are built by counting in twos
visualIdeas: a tally-marked bone beside a figure pointing to body parts in counting order

topics.title: The Roman Numerals
objectives: Student can write and read numbers in Roman numerals using I, V, X, L, C, D and M
Student can explain how 4 is written as IV (1 less than 5) and 40 as XL (10 less than 50)
visualIdeas: a table of Roman numerals with grouping into tens, fives and ones

topics.title: The Egyptian Number System
objectives: Student can explain landmark numbers as powers of 10 in the Egyptian system
Student can write numbers using Egyptian symbols for 1, 10, 100 and so on
visualIdeas: Egyptian hieroglyphs for 1, 10, 100, 1000 with a number built from them

topics.title: Variations on the Egyptian System and the Notion of Base
objectives: Student can build number systems with landmark numbers that are powers of 5 or of another number
Student can define a base-n number system
visualIdeas: landmark numbers 1, 5, 25, 125 shown as nested groups of pebbles

topics.title: Shortcomings of the Egyptian System
objectives: Student can explain why the Egyptian system needs new symbols for ever larger powers of 10
Student can explain why a place value system was the next step in the evolution of number systems
visualIdeas: a row of Egyptian symbols ending in a question mark for the next power of 10

topics.title: The Mesopotamian Number System
objectives: Student can describe the Mesopotamian base-60 (sexagesimal) place value system
Student can read a simple Mesopotamian numeral
visualIdeas: wedge-shaped symbols arranged in base-60 places

topics.title: The Mayan and Chinese Number Systems
objectives: Student can describe the Mayan place value system and its shell-shaped placeholder for zero
Student can describe Chinese rod numerals as a base-10 system for computation
visualIdeas: Mayan dots, bars and a shell beside Chinese rod numerals

topics.title: The Hindu Number System
objectives: Student can explain the Hindu number system as a base-10 place value system with ten digits including 0
Student can explain why treating 0 as a digit lets every number be written with finitely many symbols
Student can state that the system originated in India about 2000 years ago and spread across the world
visualIdeas: 375 split into 3 hundreds, 7 tens and 5 ones under place-value headings

topics.title: A Carpenter's Problem
objectives: Student can model a rectangle using two strips as its diagonals
Student can reason that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other
Student can reason that the opposite sides of a rectangle are equal and parallel
visualIdeas: two wooden strips joined at their midpoints with a thread round their ends forming a rectangle

topics.title: The Process of Finding Properties
objectives: Student can deduce a property of a quadrilateral through geometric reasoning
Student can verify a deduced property by measuring a real quadrilateral
visualIdeas: a rectangle with a deduction written beside it and a ruler checking it

topics.title: A Special Rectangle
objectives: Student can define a square as a rectangle with all sides equal
Student can explain why every square is a rectangle but not every rectangle is a square
visualIdeas: a set diagram with squares inside rectangles

topics.title: Properties of a Square
objectives: Student can list the properties of a square, including diagonals that are equal and bisect each other at 90 degrees
Student can show that the diagonals of a square bisect its angles
visualIdeas: a square with its diagonals meeting at right angles and angle halves marked

topics.title: Angles in a Quadrilateral
objectives: Student can prove that the angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees by drawing a diagonal
Student can find a missing angle of a quadrilateral
visualIdeas: quadrilateral SOME split by a diagonal into two triangles

topics.title: More Quadrilaterals with Parallel Opposite Sides
objectives: Student can construct a parallelogram using two pairs of parallel lines

visualIdeas: a parallelogram drawn from two pairs of parallel lines with equal sides marked

topics.title: Quadrilaterals with Equal Sidelengths
objectives: Student can construct a rhombus with a compass

objectives: Student can identify the quadrilateral formed by diagonals of given lengths on a geoboard

topics.title: Kite

topics.title: Sum of Consecutive Numbers
